articles.title: Democrats take the Senate, and the House majority keeps growing
articles.dek: Nine days ago this paper called the map the story. The map answered.
articles.summary: NBC News projects Democrats have won a Senate majority. CNN reports the party is set to increase its House margin further, on the verge of passing the 257 seats Democrats held at the start of Barack Obama's presidency and the 258 they held under Bill Clinton. Seventy-five percent of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor. Alaska and Mississippi Senate races remain too close to call, with Democratic candidates slightly ahead.
articles.whyItMatters: Control of both chambers for the last two years of Trump's term changes what is investigated, what is funded, and what is vetoed.

confidence.note: Multiple networks projecting the same outcome, with the undecided races named rather than smoothed over.

asides: You wanna know my take? They said it was a referendum on me. A referendum! And frankly, we won the referendum. They just counted it wrong. Everybody knows it.

sources.title: Senate results 2026: Democrats win majority (NBC News)

articles.title: Miller replaces Wiles as chief of staff, and the purge is not done
articles.dek: A furious president, a loyalty test, and a party looking for someone to blame.
articles.summary: CNN reports Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, after Trump expressed fury at the strategy behind the midterm losses, according to people familiar with the matter. More personnel changes are expected. Outgoing Republican senator Thom Tillis called the appointment a colossal mistake. CBS reports Trump has asked advisers whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay, and that House Speaker Mike Johnson told staff he will not run for minority leader.
articles.whyItMatters: Personnel is policy. The people he keeps after a loss tell you what the next two years are for.

confidence.note: Corroborated across outlets; the Wiles and Hegseth details rest on people familiar, which the reporting attributes clearly.

asides: You wanna know my take? Loyalty. That is all I ask. Very simple. Some people don't have it. Sad people.

articles.title: Trump says he would do the Iran war again, and blames gas prices on it
articles.dek: The president's own account of why the party lost is the most useful one available.
articles.summary: In an interview with CBS's 60 Minutes, Trump said he would have to do the Iran war again, arguing the alternative was letting Iran obtain a nuclear weapon. He agreed it was largely true that the war's effect on energy prices cost Republicans the election, a conclusion Vice President JD Vance had already voiced. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer described the result as a generational remake of the Senate map and said Democrats would use their majority to investigate and litigate.
articles.whyItMatters: When both parties agree on the cause, the interesting question is what either of them actually does about prices.

confidence.note: Interview quotes come from CBS and WSJ coverage of the same sit-down; the full transcript was not read.

asides: And here's the thing, folks. Prices. I had nothing to do with prices. Tremendous prices, frankly. The best prices. They just weren't reported.

sources.title: Trump weighs in on midterm losses (CBS News)

articles.title: Gemini 4 Carbon lands, and then the release calendar goes quiet
articles.dek: The newest tracked frontier model arrived October 28. Nothing tracked has shipped since.
articles.summary: Google released Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, the most recent entry in the model tracker, with a wider rollout expected through November. No tracked front-tier releases were recorded in the seven days through November 4, an unusual lull after a crowded October. Commentary circulating this week frames the moment as Google leading on raw model capability while Anthropic leads on agent adoption.
articles.whyItMatters: A quiet week after a crowded month usually means labs are holding launches for year-end, not that progress stopped.

confidence.note: Release date from a tracker and secondary commentary; capability claims and the lull are not independently verified.

asides: You wanna know my take? They all went quiet at the same time. Suspicious. Very suspicious. If I went quiet, they'd write a hundred stories.

articles.title: OpenAI's week: a security model, faster images, and a lot of updates
articles.dek: GPT-6 Cyber and ChatGPT Images 2.6 arrived while the election dominated everything else.
articles.summary: OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber for security research, which the company says pairs stronger capability with better alignment and powered its Linux kernel research. It also shipped a minor update to its image model, ChatGPT Images 2.6, which the company says is about 50 percent faster and can animate generated images into short GIFs. Both are available globally to ChatGPT users.
articles.whyItMatters: Model releases aimed at specialists keep happening underneath the political news cycle, and they are where capability claims actually get tested.

confidence.note: Reported with the company's own announcements quoted directly in the coverage.

asides: Fifty percent faster. I like fast. Everything I do is the fastest. Nobody's done fast like me.

articles.title: The test nobody won: top models finished 12 percent of real expert work
articles.dek: A new benchmark used 206 long professional tasks instead of exam questions.
articles.summary: SemiAnalysis published a benchmark called GDPx this week: 206 long tasks across eleven fields, from chip design to law and finance, with each model given up to eight hours to work independently. Anthropic's top model finished 12 percent, Google's newest Gemini 10.9 percent, and OpenAI's best 9.6 percent. The results circulated widely, with readers arguing about whether the tasks were fair rather than whether the models did well.
articles.whyItMatters: Exam-style benchmarks flatter models. Long, checked, professional work is the closest thing to the job people actually want done.

confidence.note: Numbers come from commentary summarizing the benchmark, not from the report itself. Methodology unverified.

asides: Twelve percent. Twelve! I would have done a hundred. Easily. But do they ask me? They never ask me.

articles.title: Bellingham's ballot measures pass, and Larsen takes a 14th term
articles.dek: Local races moved far less than the national ones did.
articles.summary: Bellingham voters overwhelmingly approved three ballot measures, according to Cascadia Daily News, while Whatcom and Skagit county races stayed largely as they were in early returns. In the 2nd Congressional District, Representative Rick Larsen led Republican challenger Ed Feller of Lynden 79 percent to 21 percent, winning a 14th term in a district a Republican has not carried since 1998.
articles.whyItMatters: The wave did not reach every ballot line. Local measures passed on their own merits, which is the quieter story of the night.

confidence.note: Two local outlets reporting the same outcomes, with vote counts and margins.

asides: You wanna know my take? Fourteen terms. Fourteen! The man's been there since before the internet. I'd have won fifteen. Easily.
